summary: Defines an architecture for Open Pluggable Edge Services, in which a data provider, a data consumer and optional intermediary entities cooperate to apply services to a data stream. It describes the building blocks that let services be inserted at network edges.

plainLanguage.summary: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) describes how an extra service can act on a data stream between its provider and consumer. It explains the parts that choose and run the service, and the safeguards that make the processing visible and authorized.

subtitle: A framework for adding cooperating services to a data stream between its provider and consumer.

tldr.problem: Some data-stream services need an application entity between the provider and consumer to analyze or transform their exchange.
tldr.mechanism: OPES uses service applications, data dispatchers, and rules to decide when services act on a flow. A dispatcher may also send work to a callout server.
tldr.outcome: The framework requires consent, addressability, tracing, and trust-aware handling. It leaves most interoperability details to a ruleset schema and callout-protocol specifications.

today: RFC 3835 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Add a Service to a Data Stream
sections.content:
A provider and consumer may need another application entity to customize a data stream. For example, a service could adapt a stream to a consumer's available display capabilities. Placing the service between the endpoints can be useful and, for some services, may be the only deployment option.

This memo presents the architecture for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES). HTTP is used as an example of the protocol carrying the data, but the architecture is described as largely independent of that application protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A service may need to change or examine data while it travels from its provider to its consumer. OPES describes how an intermediary can do that as part of the service.

sections.title: Entities, Flows, and Rules
sections.content:
The architecture has three related concepts: OPES entities, OPES flows, and OPES rules. A service application analyzes and may transform messages. A data dispatcher applies a ruleset and invokes the relevant service application. An OPES processor contains these functions and MUST include a data dispatcher.

An OPES flow is a cooperative exchange among a provider, a consumer, zero or more service applications, and at least one data dispatcher. Rules combine conditions and actions to determine which services operate on a flow. The ruleset must have an unambiguous result; its schema is standardized, while the method used to configure it is local to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: A dispatcher reads rules to decide which service should handle a data flow. A processor needs a dispatcher, and the rules must lead to a clear decision.

sections.title: Callout Servers and Tracing
sections.content:
A processor can delegate service execution to one or more callout servers. The dispatcher communicates with them using the OPES callout protocol (OCP). OCP does not need to understand the meaning of the application data, while the dispatcher uses service-aware processing to send data to the correct local or remote service.

Each dispatcher MUST support tracing so its work can be checked. Tracing is to be feasible on the flow, for each processor, through in-band annotation. Header extensions may be needed, but the presence of an OPES processor SHALL NOT interfere with clients or servers that do not know about OPES.
sections.plainLanguage: A dispatcher may send work to a separate service server. Each dispatcher must also make it possible to trace what happened to the flow.

sections.title: Consent, Trust, and Privacy
sections.content:
The provider and consumer are the primary stakeholders. They need a trust policy that identifies who may handle data and what protections communications require. Trust can be delegated step by step, creating a trust domain; a processor may belong to more than one such domain and must be able to report its memberships for tracing.

Processors MUST be addressable at the IP layer by the consumer and MUST have consent from either the provider or consumer. Callout servers need to follow the applicable policy. The memo recommends strong authentication and message protection for callout communication, requires per-flow privacy information, and describes digital signatures as one way to mark changes for later verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider or consumer must agree to OPES processing. The parties must also know which services they trust and how those services handle private data.

sections.title: Interoperability and IAB Considerations
sections.content:
The framework addresses concerns about one-party consent, IP-layer addressability, notification, non-blocking behavior, privacy, and the impact of transformations on references. It says documentation should identify transformations, and describes HTTP extensions that could let a consumer request a version without OPES services.

The memo concludes that the architecture itself has few interoperability requirements. It identifies a standardized ruleset schema and the requirements for the OPES callout protocol as the necessary shared elements. The document is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture aims to make processing authorized and visible while allowing ordinary clients and servers to keep working. It leaves the shared rules format and callout requirements to related specifications.
